title: Eclipses
subtitle: When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up exactly, and how to watch safely

sections.heading: Two kinds of shadow
body: After this lesson you will be able to say what is happening during a lunar and a solar eclipse, why they are uncommon, and how to watch each one safely.

A lunar eclipse happens at full Moon, when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow. Everyone on the night side of Earth sees it at the same moment. A solar eclipse happens at new Moon, when the Moon passes in front of the Sun and its shadow falls on Earth. That shadow is small, so only people in the right place see it.

Earth's shadow has two parts. The umbra is the dark core where the Sun is completely hidden. The penumbra is the pale outer zone where only part of the Sun is blocked. A Moon that passes only through the penumbra dims so slightly that most people notice nothing. When part of it enters the umbra you see a dark curved bite: a partial eclipse. When all of it is inside, the eclipse is total.

A totally eclipsed Moon does not vanish. It turns a dim copper red, because Earth's atmosphere bends a little sunlight into the shadow and filters out the blue on the way. You are seeing the glow of every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once. Totality can last more than an hour, and a lunar eclipse is completely safe to watch with eyes, binoculars or a telescope.

demo.title: A total lunar eclipse over Brooklyn

steps.caption: June 25, 2029, 9:32 pm in Brooklyn. The full Moon is low in the southeast, 10° up, as its edge first touches the umbra. Over the next hour a dark bite spreads across it.
10:30 pm: totality begins. The whole Moon is now inside Earth's shadow and glows red, 17° above the horizon in Sagittarius. With the moonlight gone, the stars around it come out.

11:22 pm: mid-eclipse, 21° up in the south-southeast. Totality lasts an unusually long 1 hour 43 minutes or so, until 12:13 am, and the last of the umbra leaves the Moon at 1:12 am. All of it is visible from Brooklyn.

Sooner, but slighter: on January 11, 2028 at 11:13 pm the Moon, 69° high in Gemini, just clips the umbra, and a small dark notch shows on its edge for about an hour. This is the first umbral lunar eclipse visible from Brooklyn after 2026.

figures.caption: Earth's shadow has a dark core, the umbra, inside a pale fringe, the penumbra. Move the Moon through it on different paths: through the middle it turns copper red, off centre a dark bite appears, and in the penumbra alone it barely dims. Switch to Solar to see how small the Moon's shadow is on Earth.

image.alt: A diagonal row of nine pictures of the totally eclipsed Moon, each a coppery red disc with darker markings
image.kindNote: Several exposures taken during totality, combined into one sequence

figures.caption: The total lunar eclipse of 3–4 March 2007, as the Moon crossed Earth's umbra. It never vanished: light bent and reddened by Earth's atmosphere kept it glowing copper red throughout totality.

thinkAbout.question: What would an astronaut standing on the Moon see during a total lunar eclipse?
thinkAbout.answer: A total eclipse of the Sun by Earth. Earth would look like a black disc nearly four times wider than the Sun, with a thin glowing red ring around its edge: the light of every sunrise and sunset on Earth at that moment. That red light is what colours the Moon.

sections.heading: Why not every month
body: There is a new Moon and a full Moon every month, yet most months pass without an eclipse. The reason is that the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to the plane of Earth's orbit. At most new Moons the Moon passes above or below the Sun, and at most full Moons it misses Earth's shadow, which is less than three Moon-widths across at that distance.

The Moon crosses the plane of Earth's orbit, the ecliptic, at two points called nodes. An eclipse can happen only when a new or full Moon falls near a node. The name ecliptic comes from this: it is the line where eclipses occur. The nodes are lined up with the Sun twice a year, about six months apart, and each alignment opens an eclipse season about five weeks long. Every season brings at least one solar and one lunar eclipse somewhere on Earth, two weeks apart, though many are partial or penumbral.

steps.caption: The Moon each evening from April 10 to 19, 2027, against the ecliptic line. It starts almost 5° north of the line, crosses it at a node on April 14–15, and ends more than 4° south. The crossing came at half phase, a week from new or full, so April 2027 has no eclipse.

figures.caption: The Moon's orbit is tilted to Earth's, crossing it at two nodes. That line of nodes keeps nearly the same direction in space, so it points at the Sun only about twice a year. Play 2027: most new and full Moons pass above or below the Sun's line, but in February and in July–August the nodes line up and the eclipses come in pairs.

misconception.myth: There should be a solar eclipse at every new Moon and a lunar eclipse at every full Moon.
misconception.fact: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so at most new and full Moons it passes above or below the Sun or Earth's shadow. Eclipses happen only in the eclipse seasons, when a new or full Moon falls near a node: twice a year, with two or three eclipses each time.

check.prompt: In 2027 the eclipse seasons fall in February and in July–August. When is the next one?
choices: Around January 2028
Around May 2028
Around February 2029
There is no pattern
check.explanation: Eclipse seasons come about every six months, and a little earlier each year because the line of nodes slowly turns. The next one brings a partial lunar eclipse on 12 January 2028 and an annular solar eclipse on 26 January 2028.

sections.heading: Solar eclipses and your eyes
body: By coincidence the Moon and the Sun appear almost exactly the same size in our sky. When the Moon passes centrally across the Sun and is near enough to cover it, the eclipse is total along a narrow track, usually 100 miles wide or less, for at most a few minutes. The sky darkens and the Sun's pearly outer atmosphere, the corona, appears. When the Moon is in the farther part of its orbit it looks slightly too small and leaves a ring of Sun showing: an annular eclipse. Over a much wider region either side of the track, the eclipse is partial.

Safety matters here. Never look at the Sun without proper protection, not even when most of it is covered. The remaining sliver can burn the retina without any pain. Use eclipse glasses or handheld viewers certified to the ISO 12312-2 standard; ordinary sunglasses are useless. Binoculars and telescopes must have a solar filter made for the purpose fixed over the front of the instrument. Never look through one while wearing eclipse glasses, because the concentrated light will burn through them. A pinhole projecting the Sun's image onto paper is always safe. The only time you may look with bare eyes is during the brief total phase of a total eclipse, and a partial eclipse has no such phase.

steps.caption: Brooklyn, January 14, 2029, 12:50 pm, with the blue sky removed. The new Moon covers about 40% of the Sun's disc, 27° up in the south. This partial eclipse runs from 11:25 am to 2:10 pm and is the next substantial solar eclipse for Brooklyn. Eye protection is needed throughout.

Luxor, Egypt, August 2, 2027, 1:05 pm local time. The Moon covers the Sun completely, 82° up, almost overhead, for about 6 minutes 20 seconds: one of the longest totalities of the century. None of this eclipse can be seen from Brooklyn.

figures.caption: The Moon's distance swings between about 357,000 and 407,000 km, so its disc grows and shrinks a little against the Sun's. Near enough, it covers the Sun completely and its dark shadow reaches the ground: a total eclipse. Farther away it leaves a ring: an annular eclipse.

images.alt: A black Moon covering the Sun completely, surrounded by the white glow of the corona, with tiny pink spots at the edge
images.label: Total: the corona
images.kindNote: From a NASA aircraft 25,000 feet above the Oregon coast, 21 August 2017; cropped

images.alt: A thin bright ring of sunlight around the dark disc of the Moon on a black background
images.label: Annular: a ring of Sun

figures.caption: Left: totality on 21 August 2017, when the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, the corona, appears. Right: an annular eclipse, with the Moon a little too far away to cover the Sun. Only the brief total phase is safe to look at without a solar filter.

thinkAbout.question: Will total solar eclipses happen forever?
thinkAbout.answer: No. The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth, by about 4 cm a year. Many millions of years from now it will always look smaller than the Sun, and every central eclipse will be annular. We happen to live at a time when the two discs match.

sections.tryIt: Open the Events page and find the next lunar eclipse visible from your location. Put it in your calendar now. A lunar eclipse needs no equipment and no dark sky: it works perfectly well from a Brooklyn stoop.

keyPoints: Lunar eclipse: full Moon in Earth's shadow, seen from the whole night side. Solar eclipse: new Moon in front of the Sun, seen from a limited area.
The Moon's orbit is tilted 5°, so eclipses happen only when a new or full Moon falls near a node, in eclipse seasons about six months apart.
The totally eclipsed Moon is red from sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere.
Lunar eclipses are safe to watch. For the Sun, use ISO 12312-2 eclipse glasses, and front-mounted solar filters on any binoculars or telescope.

questions.prompt: Why is there not a lunar eclipse at every full Moon?
choices: Earth's shadow is too faint most months
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so it usually passes above or below Earth's shadow
The Moon is usually too far away
Lunar eclipses happen only in winter
questions.explanation: Only when a full Moon occurs near a node, where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic, does it pass through the shadow.

questions.prompt: At which phase of the Moon can a solar eclipse happen?
choices: Full Moon
First quarter
Any phase
New Moon
questions.explanation: The Moon must be between Earth and the Sun to cover it, and that is new Moon.

questions.prompt: Why does the Moon turn red during a total lunar eclipse?
choices: Sunlight bent and reddened by Earth's atmosphere reaches it inside the shadow
The Moon heats up
Mars reflects red light onto it
Its surface is naturally red and only then visible
questions.explanation: The atmosphere scatters away blue light and bends the remaining red light into the umbra.

questions.prompt: You want to look at a partial solar eclipse through binoculars. What is the safe way?
choices: Wear eclipse glasses and look through the binoculars
Wear good sunglasses
Fit certified solar filters over the front lenses of the binoculars
Look only for a second at a time
questions.explanation: The filter must cut the light before it enters the optics. Eclipse glasses behind binoculars receive concentrated sunlight and can fail instantly.

questions.prompt: A total lunar eclipse is under way. Who can see it?
choices: Only people on a narrow track
Only people at the equator
Everyone on the side of Earth where the Moon is above the horizon
Only people with telescopes
questions.explanation: The Moon really is darkened, so the whole night side of Earth sees the same eclipse at the same time.

questions.prompt: What is an annular solar eclipse?
choices: One where the Moon looks slightly too small to cover the Sun and leaves a ring
One that happens every year
One seen only in the penumbra
One that takes place at night
questions.explanation: When the Moon is in the more distant part of its orbit its disc is smaller than the Sun's and a ring, or annulus, of sunlight remains.
